doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Mother's Catholicism and tuberculosis; his 1994 lung cancer
summary: His mother, a Catholic, also died of tuberculosis. He recounts surviving lung cancer in 1994 without chemotherapy and the surgeon who said he would play again.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well, my mother had adopted Catholicism, and also the first black Catholic Church in this country. They had one…in Chicago, they say there was the first one, but this had a small congregation. She was just the opposite of him from what I gathered, you know? She also died of tuberculosis. Therefore, years later, 1994, when I developed this lung cancer and walked away from it, thanks to God, without Chemo or anything. I’m a poster boy for the cancer society. I don’t smoke or drink. Now, I did drink, but the message is I was the cardiac king with Wayne Shorter. That led the cancer of course, so be it. I’ve never one to obsess anything.
So, you think it just could have been a vulnerability that was in your family?
I think it was a thing that was in my genes. Both parents were susceptible to it, too. They said, “Has anybody in your family has tuberculosis?” They thought that’s what it was.

In the 90’s, which is a long way from now. But, I walked through it. A brilliant heart surgeon, four feet tall, he said, “Curtis, we got it in. The good news is you will play again.” He was already a fan; his wife was a fan.
What was his name, the surgeon’s name?
Uh, what was his name? I started to say O’Hara, that wasn’t his name. I’ll figure it out.
